title: Files and Folders
about: Find files, read their types, and tell local files from cloud ones.

cards.prompt: Everything you save is a **file**. Files go in **folders**, and folders can sit inside other folders, like boxes inside boxes. The route to a file is its **path**. Here, `volcanoes.docx` is inside `Science`, which is inside `School`, which is inside `Documents`. Put its path in order, from the **biggest folder** (the one holding everything else) to the file.
cards.explanation: A path goes from the biggest box inwards: `Documents > School > Science > volcanoes.docx`. The file itself always comes last.
cards.hint: Think of boxes inside boxes: start with the biggest box that holds everything, then go inwards.
cards.nudge: A path goes from the biggest folder inwards, one box at a time. The file itself always comes last.

cards.title: Extensions
cards.body:
The end of a file's name, after the **last** dot, is its **extension**. It tells the OS what kind of file it is, and which app opens it.

`.jpg` is a photo, `.mp3` a song and `.mp4` a video. `.exe` is a **program**: opening it *runs* it, so only open ones you trust.

cards.prompt: Match each [[extension]] to the kind of file it marks.

pairs.right: A program that runs when opened

cards.explanation: `.jpg` is a photo, `.mp3` a song and `.mp4` a video. `.exe` is different: it's a **program**. Opening it *runs* it, so only open ones you trust.
cards.hint: The extension tells the OS what kind of file it is. Think back to the list: photos, songs, videos and programs.
cards.nudge: Look again at the letters: `.mp3` and `.mp4` look alike but mark different things, and one extension means a program.

cards.prompt: Label what each file really is. Read to the **last** dot.
cards.explanation: `holiday.jpg` is a photo and `song.mp3` a song. `photo.jpg.exe` ends in **.exe**, so it's a program, whatever the `.jpg` in the middle says.
cards.hint: Read each file name right to the end. Only the [[extension]] after the **last** dot counts.
cards.nudge: A name can have more than one dot. Ignore anything in the middle and look only at what comes after the last dot.

cards.prompt: A website promised free holiday wallpapers. You clicked download.

steps.text: Your Downloads folder now has a new file: `photo.jpg.exe`. What is it?

choices.consequence: Only the **last** [[extension]] counts. The `.jpg` in the middle is a disguise.

choices.text: A program pretending to be a photo
choices.consequence: Right. It ends in **.exe**, so opening it would run it.

steps.text: What do you do with it?

choices.text: Open it once, just to check what it is
choices.consequence: Opening a program runs it, and it only takes one run for it to do harm.

choices.text: Send it to a friend to try
choices.consequence: Now your friend's device is at risk too. Never pass on a file you don't trust.

choices.text: Delete it without opening it, and tell an adult you trust
choices.consequence: The file is gone, and they can check nothing else came with it.

cards.explanation: Read to the **last** dot. `photo.jpg.exe` is a program in disguise. Some computers hide the last extension, so it might even show as `photo.jpg`. Delete files like this without opening them, and tell a parent, teacher or other adult you trust.
cards.hint: Read the file name right to the last dot. What does that extension mean happens when you open it?

cards.prompt: Saving to **the cloud** means storing a file on a company's **server**: a powerful computer in a data centre, reached over the internet. The cloud isn't in the sky. It's someone else's computer, in a building with very serious air conditioning. Where is each file stored?

items.label: A song downloaded to play offline
A drawing saved to the laptop's storage
A shared doc you edit in a web browser
Emails in a web mail inbox
A game save kept in your online account

cards.explanation: Files you **downloaded** or **saved to the device** are in its storage. Files you reach through a **website or online account** live on the company's servers, in the cloud.
cards.hint: Ask yourself: did you download or save it to the device, or do you reach it through a website or online account?
cards.nudge: Files downloaded or saved to the device live in its storage. Files you reach through a website or account live on a company's server.

cards.prompt: You're on a plane with no Wi-Fi, and you want to work on your essay. It's saved **only in the cloud**.

choices.text: Yes: it's my file, so my laptop already has it
choices.consequence: The file lives on a company's server, not in your laptop's storage. With no internet, the laptop can't reach it.

choices.text: Yes: cloud files reach you through the air, anywhere
choices.consequence: The cloud isn't in the sky. It's a server in a building, and you can only reach it over the internet.

choices.text: No: I need the internet to reach the server it's on
choices.consequence: Right. No internet, no essay. Time for the in-flight movie.

steps.text: Next time you fly, how can you work on it without Wi-Fi?

choices.text: Download a copy to the laptop before the flight
choices.consequence: A copy in the laptop's storage opens anywhere. Back online, you can save your changes to the cloud again.

choices.text: Save it to the cloud twice, so there's a spare copy
choices.consequence: Two copies on the server are still on the server. You need one in the laptop's own storage.

cards.explanation: Cloud files live on a company's [[servers|server]], so you need the internet to reach them. Keep a copy on your device when you'll be offline.
cards.hint: Where does a cloud-only file really live, and what do you need to reach it?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Folders hold files. The **path** is the route to a file.
- The **extension** after the last dot says what it is. `.exe` runs.
- **Cloud** files live on a server you reach over the internet.

That's the software side. Next module: fixing things yourself.
